title: Writing a threaded program
objective: By the end of this lesson you can create threads, pass each one its own data, collect results, and avoid the two mistakes that make almost every first threaded program wrong.

blocks.text: The interface is small: create a thread, wait for it, and optionally get a value back. The mistakes are also small, and both of them are about lifetime — what the thread is allowed to point at, and how long that thing lives.

blocks.caption: The whole interface, in one program
lines: int ids[4];                       /* one slot per thread — this matters */
pthread_join(t[i], NULL);     /* wait for each to finish */

blocks.text: Build it with -pthread — that flag is required both to compile and to link, and forgetting it produces confusing errors rather than a clear message. gcc -pthread prog.c -o prog is the command.
Mistake one: every thread pointing at the same variable

blocks.caption: Wrong, and why
lines: /* Every thread receives the address of the SAME i.
By the time a thread reads it, the loop has moved on — or finished.
Typical result: several threads all report id 4. */

blocks.text: The array version above is correct because each thread receives the address of a different element, and that array outlives every thread because main is still running. The rule generalises: whatever you hand a thread must remain valid for as long as the thread might read it.
Mistake two: pointing at a stack frame that returns

blocks.caption: A dangling pointer, delivered by a thread
lines: }   /* <- spawn returns HERE; value is gone; the thread may still be running */
/*   2. Own it: malloc the argument, and let the thread free it     */
/*   3. Outlive it: use storage that lives long enough (static, or */
/*      an array in a caller that waits)                           */

blocks.title: This is the C course's dangling pointer, in a new setting
blocks.text: You already know that returning a pointer to a local is a bug. Threads make it worse in one specific way: the function returns successfully and the corruption happens elsewhere, later, in a different thread. Address sanitizer still catches it — build with -fsanitize=address -g, exactly as in the C course.

blocks.caption: Returning a value from a thread
lines: long *result = malloc(sizeof *result);   /* heap: outlives this function */
pthread_join(t, (void **)&answer);        /* join hands you the return value */
free(answer);                             /* the joiner owns it now */

blocks.text: Join or detach — pick one for every thread

rows: Resources leak — the thread stays a zombie
You need the result or the timing

blocks.title: A joinable thread nobody joins is a leak
blocks.text: It is the thread version of the zombie from the process module, and it has the same fix: collect it, or say up front that you never will. pthread_detach(t) makes the second choice explicit. A long-running program that creates joinable threads and never joins them will exhaust memory.

blocks.title: Write it, then break it deliberately
steps: Build the four-worker program above: gcc -pthread -Wall prog.c -o prog
Run it several times and note that the output order changes between runs
Now change &ids[i] to &i and run it repeatedly — watch ids repeat or all show 4
Put that back, and write the spawn() function that returns while its thread is still running
Rebuild with: gcc -pthread -Wall -g -fsanitize=address prog.c -o prog  and run it
Read the sanitizer report — it names the freed stack frame
Make a thread return a malloc'd result and collect it with pthread_join
Create 1000 joinable threads without joining them, watch memory, then add pthread_detach and compare
blocks.expected: Changing output order is your first direct evidence that you no longer control execution order. The &i version shows why every thread needs its own argument, and the sanitizer names the stack-lifetime bug precisely. The last step reproduces the process module's zombie problem in thread form.

cheatsheet: Build with -pthread (needed for both compiling and linking)
pthread_create(&t, NULL, fn, arg) — fn takes and returns void *
pthread_join(t, &ret) waits and collects the return value
Give each thread its OWN argument — never the loop variable's address
Whatever you pass must outlive the thread: join, or malloc, or use longer-lived storage
Return a value by returning a heap pointer; the joiner frees it
Joinable threads must be joined or they leak — pthread_detach if you never will
Output order changes between runs; that is normal and is the point
-fsanitize=address catches thread lifetime bugs, same as in the C course

checkpoint.prompt: A loop creates four threads, passing &i each time. Several print the same id. Why?

choices.B: All four received the address of the same variable, which the loop keeps changing
choices.D: The threads ran in the wrong order

checkpoint.explanation: They share one variable. Give each thread its own storage — an array element, or a malloc'd copy.

checkpoint.prompt: A function creates a thread, passes it the address of a local, and returns immediately. What is the defect?

choices.A: Nothing, if the thread is fast enough
choices.B: The local's stack frame is gone once the function returns, so the thread may read freed memory

checkpoint.explanation: 'Fast enough' is not a guarantee, it is a race you usually win. Join before returning, or hand the thread memory it owns.

checkpoint.prompt: A server creates a joinable thread per request and never joins them. What happens over time?

choices.A: Nothing — threads clean up on exit
choices.B: Resources for each finished thread are retained, and the process eventually exhausts memory
choices.C: The scheduler slows down but memory is fine
choices.D: New threads silently fail to start immediately

checkpoint.explanation: It is the zombie problem again: a finished joinable thread keeps its record until someone collects it. Join it, or detach it up front.

checkpoint.prompt: You run the same threaded program five times and get five different output orders. What does that tell you?

choices.B: Nothing is guaranteeing an order — which is normal, and is exactly why shared data needs coordination

checkpoint.explanation: Order is not part of the contract unless you create one. That is the observation the next lesson turns into a bug you can measure.
